title: Local etale valuation factors and their residue generators
statement: Let $R$ be a henselian valuation domain [def-trf-valuation-ring, def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], with fraction field $K$ [def-weil-field], maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and residue field $k=R/\mathfrak m$. Let $D$ be a commutative $R$-algebra with $\operatorname{Spec}D\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ etale [def-weil-etale-morphism], and let $\mathfrak n\subset D$ be prime with $\mathfrak n\cap R=\mathfrak m$. Then $S=D_{\mathfrak n}$ is a direct factor of $D$ as an $R$-algebra, is finite etale over $R$, and is a valuation domain. Its fraction field $L$ is finite separable over $K$ [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension]. The ring $S$ is the integral closure of $R$ in $L$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] and the unique valuation ring of $L$ extending $R$. Its maximal ideal is $\mathfrak mS$, its residue field $l=S/\mathfrak mS$ is finite separable over $k$, and $S$ is free of rank $[L:K]=[l:k]$ over $R$. For every $y\in S$ such that $l=k(\bar y)$, one has $S=R[y]$ and $L=K(y)$. The monic minimal polynomial $g\in K[T]$ of $y$ belongs to $R[T]$, has degree $[l:k]$, reduces to the minimal polynomial of $\bar y$ over $k$, and $g'(y)$ is a unit of $S$. No Noetherian or discrete-valuation hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tags 04GH (lemma-finite-over-henselian) and 04GK (lemma-henselian-cat-finite-etale), valuation-ring specialization and residue-power-basis calculation used in Temkin Proposition 2.2.1, proof, pp. 11--12.

proof.text: $D$ is a finitely generated $R$-algebra by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-algebra-finite-presentation-localization]. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-henselian-finite-type-product-decomposition] to write $D\simeq A_1\times\cdots\times A_t\times B$, where each $A_i$ is local and finite over $R$ and $B$ has no quasi-finite prime over $\mathfrak m$. Each displayed factor is the localization $D_e$ at its identity idempotent $e$, hence is etale over $R$ by the same localization lemma. By [lem-weil-pbc-etale-quotient-base-change] and [lem-weil-pbc-etale-algebra-over-field-product], its quotient by $\mathfrak m$ is a finite product of finite separable $k$-fields. Each prime of such a product is isolated: its singleton is the basic open of the corresponding identity idempotent. Thus every prime of $B$ above $\mathfrak m$ would be quasi-finite by [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime], a contradiction. The prime $\mathfrak n$ therefore occurs in one $A_i$.

source.place: Tags 04GJ (lemma-mop-up), 04GH (lemma-finite-over-henselian), proof of (3), and 00U3 (lemma-etale-over-field); finite-type product decomposition and exclusion of the residual factor.

proof.text: The prime of $A_i$ corresponding to $\mathfrak n$ contains $\mathfrak mA_i$, so $A_i/\mathfrak mA_i$ is nonzero. It is local, being a proper quotient of a local ring. The field-product description in step 1 forces this quotient to have exactly one factor, hence to be a field. Consequently the prime in question is $\mathfrak mA_i$, the maximal ideal of $A_i$. Localizing a local ring at its maximal ideal changes nothing, since all the denominators are already units. Localizing the product at $\mathfrak n$ kills the other identity idempotents. Therefore the canonical localization $D\to S=D_{\mathfrak n}$ is, under this product decomposition, the projection to $A_i$. In particular $S$ is a direct factor, is finite etale over $R$, and $\mathfrak mS$ is its maximal ideal; the quotient $l$ is finite separable over $k$.

source.place: Tags 04GH and 04GK (lemma-henselian-cat-finite-etale), initial proof paragraph: identification of a local factor and its residue field. Explicit product and localization calculation.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-etale-localization-valuation-domain] directly to $R\to D$ and $\mathfrak n$. Its hypotheses hold because $R$ is a valuation domain and the contraction of $\mathfrak n$ is exactly its maximal ideal. It gives an injective local map $R\to S$ and makes $S$ a valuation domain. In particular we may regard both rings as subrings of $L=\operatorname{Frac}(S)$ and embed $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ into $L$.

By [lem-weil-pbc-etale-algebra-flat], $S$ is flat over $R$. Apply [lem-trf-valuation-finite-type-module-presentation] with $A=B=R$ and $M=S$: the identity ring map is of finite type, $S$ is a finite $R$-module by step 2, and its flatness is established. Thus $S$ is finitely presented as an $R$-module. It is torsion-free because $R\to S$ is injective and $S$ is a domain. By [lem-sc-valuation-fp-torsionfree-free] it is free of a finite rank $r$. Reducing any such basis gives a basis of $S/\mathfrak mS=l$ over $k$: the isomorphism $S\simeq R^r$ quotients to $l\simeq k^r$. Thus $r=[l:k]\ge1$.

source.place: Tag 053E(2), lemma-flat-finite-type-valuation-ring-finite-presentation, specialized to the identity algebra; finite free reduction calculation.

proof.text: Let $C=(R\setminus\{0\})^{-1}S=K\otimes_RS$. Step 3 makes this a subring of $L$ and a domain. Localizing the basis of step 4 gives a $K$-basis of $C$ of size $r$. For $0\ne c\in C$, multiplication by $c$ is an injective endomorphism of this finite-dimensional space, hence surjective; in particular $cd=1$ for some $d\in C$. Thus $C$ is a field containing $S$, so $C=L$ by the fraction-field universal property. It follows that $[L:K]=r=[l:k]$. By [lem-weil-pbc-etale-ring-base-change], $C$ is etale over $K$; [lem-weil-pbc-etale-algebra-over-field-product] then identifies this nonzero field with one finite separable field factor. Hence $L/K$ is finite separable.

source.place: Tag 00U3 (lemma-etale-over-field), generic-fibre application after base change; fraction-field identification by finite-dimensional multiplication.

proof.text: For any $s\in S$, apply [lem-weil-cayley-hamilton-free-module] to multiplication by $s$ on the rank-$r$ free module $S$. Evaluating the resulting endomorphism identity at $1$ gives a monic polynomial in $R[T]$ annihilating $s$. Thus all of $S$ is integral over $R$. Conversely, if $z\in L$ is integral over $R$, its monic equation also has coefficients in $S$, so it is integral over $S$. By [lem-weil-pbc-valuation-ring-normal] applied to the valuation domain $S$, one has $z\in S$. These two inclusions identify $S$ with the integral closure of $R$ in $L$. Applying the same normality lemma to $R$ also gives $S\cap K=R$: an element of that intersection is integral over $R$ and lies in its fraction field.

source.place: Tag 00DX (lemma-charpoly), and Tag 00IC (lemma-valuation-ring-normal): integrality via the multiplication endomorphism and the two inclusions for integral closure.

proof.text: Let $W\subseteq L$ be any valuation ring extending $R$, meaning $W\cap K=R$. Every element of $S$ is integral over $R\subseteq W$, so normality of $W$ from [lem-weil-pbc-valuation-ring-normal] implies $S\subseteq W$. Moreover $\mathfrak m_W\cap R=\mathfrak m$: a unit of $R$ stays a unit, whereas if $0\ne a\in\mathfrak m$ were a unit in $W$, then $a^{-1}\in W\cap K=R$, a contradiction. Hence the proper prime $\mathfrak m_W\cap S$ contains the maximal ideal $\mathfrak mS$ and equals it. If $z\in W\setminus S$, the valuation property of $S$ gives $z^{-1}\in S$; it cannot be a unit in $S$, so $z^{-1}\in\mathfrak mS\subseteq\mathfrak m_W$. This contradicts $z\in W$. Thus $W=S$, proving uniqueness without a discreteness or height assumption.

source.place: Tag 00IC (lemma-valuation-ring-normal) and the defining inverse alternative for a valuation ring; explicit uniqueness argument for the integral finite local factor.

proof.text: Fix $y\in S$ with $l=k(\bar y)$ and write $r=[l:k]$. By [lem-weil-pbc-simple-algebraic-extension-power-basis], $1,\bar y,\ldots,\bar y^{r-1}$ is a $k$-basis of $l$. The module $S$ is finite and $R$ is local, so [lem-weil-pbc-nakayama-local-generators] implies that $1,y,\ldots,y^{r-1}$ spans $S$ over $R$. It is actually a basis: in a chosen rank-$r$ basis of $S$ its column matrix reduces to an invertible matrix over $k$; its determinant is therefore outside $\mathfrak m$ and a unit in $R$, so the adjugate gives an inverse over $R$. Consequently $S=R[y]$. Localizing gives $L=K\otimes_RS=K[y]$, and thus $L=K(y)$.

source.place: Tag 00DV (lemma-NAK), (8); the residue power basis and determinant calculation for its lifts. This supplies the residue-generator computation mentioned in the item source.

proof.text: Write $y^r=-\sum_{j<r}a_jy^j$ in this basis, with $a_j\in R$, and set $h=T^r+\sum_{j<r}a_jT^j\in R[T]$. Its coefficientwise image in $K[T]$ annihilates $y$. No nonzero polynomial of degree below $r$ can do so, since the localized powers are a $K$-basis of $L$. Monic division by $h$ therefore shows that this image is exactly the monic minimal polynomial $g$ of $y$ over $K$. Reducing the displayed relation and using the residue power basis shows that $\bar h$ is the monic minimal polynomial of $\bar y$ over $k$, also of degree $r$. This polynomial is separable because $l/k$ is separable [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension]. By [def-pc-separable-polynomial], there exist $U,V\in k[T]$ with $U\bar h+V\bar h^{\prime}=1$. Evaluating at $\bar y$ proves $\bar h^{\prime}(\bar y)\ne0$. The residue of $h^{\prime}(y)$ is this value, since reduction commutes termwise with differentiation and evaluation. Thus $g^{\prime}(y)=h^{\prime}(y)$ lies outside the maximal ideal of the local ring $S$ and is a unit. This proves every polynomial clause.

source.place: Fields, Tag 09H1 (definition-separable), and Algebra, Tag 00U3 (lemma-etale-over-field), power-basis/minimal-polynomial calculation.

proof_origin.place: Assembly of Tags 04GJ, 04GH and 00U3 with more-algebra.tex Tags 0ASJ and 053E(2), and the explicit residue-power-basis calculation; Temkin is not locally available.
